patients.summary: Regional sales manager with type 2 diabetes, hypertension and rheumatoid arthritis on long-term low-dose prednisone who joins the practice in June 2025 right after a travel-provoked left popliteal DVT. A second, iliofemoral DVT after a transatlantic flight in November 2025 puts her on indefinite apixaban. On the day of her last practice visit in June 2026 she falls at home and is admitted to the ICU with adrenal crisis.

Records release signed electronically for her former primary care office; request faxed today.

conditions.label: Acute deep vein thrombosis of left popliteal vein

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets (10 mg) by mouth twice daily for 7 days, then 1 tablet (5 mg) twice daily

reports.text: Left lower extremity venous duplex. Indication: left calf pain and swelling. Grayscale compression, color and spectral flow were assessed from the common femoral vein to the calf. The common femoral, femoral and proximal deep femoral veins compress fully with normal phasic flow and augmentation. The left popliteal vein is distended with echogenic intraluminal material and does not compress. The posterior tibial and peroneal veins compress where seen. The great saphenous vein is patent. Contralateral common femoral vein shows normal respiratory phasicity.
reports.conclusion: Acute deep vein thrombosis of the left popliteal vein.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record (received)
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital emergency department. Date of service 06/09/2025. Received by fax 06/11/2025.

CC: L lower leg pain and swelling.

HPI: 54F with T2DM, HTN and RA on chronic low-dose prednisone. Three days of left calf pain and swelling that has steadily worsened. Drove about 9 hours each way for a work trip roughly two weeks ago. Denies any injury to the leg. No chest pain, no dyspnea, no hemoptysis.

Meds: metformin, lisinopril, prednisone 5 mg daily. Allergies: NKDA.
PSH: TAH 2010, R carpal tunnel release 2015.
FH: father DVT at 62; mother RA; maternal grandmother T2DM.
SH: never smoker, wine socially, 1-2 glasses a week. Regional sales manager.

Exam: VS within normal limits throughout stay. L calf erythematous, warm, tender. Pitting edema from the ankle up to mid-calf. Calf circumference 3 cm greater on the left than the right. Distal pulses intact. Heart and lungs normal. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

Labs: BMP with normal renal function; CBC unremarkable.
Imaging: venous duplex, L popliteal vein noncompressible, consistent with DVT.

MDM: Provoked L popliteal DVT (prolonged car travel). Hemodynamically normal, no signs of PE. Normal renal function, no bleeding history. Suitable for outpatient anticoagulation.

Disposition: discharged home. Apixaban 10 mg BID x 7 days then 5 mg BID; anticipate a 3 month course, duration per PCP. Leg elevation, walk as tolerated. Return for chest pain, shortness of breath or bleeding. Pt reports she has a new PCP visit on 6/20.

documents.title: Went to the ER yesterday
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, I'm a new patient, my first appointment is the 20th. I ended up in the ER yesterday afternoon with my left leg and they found a blood clot behind the knee. They started me on Eliquis. Should I keep the appointment on the 20th or come in sooner? I'm supposed to drive to a client meeting on Thursday.

documents.title: RE: Went to the ER yesterday
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Valerie, welcome, and sorry this was your introduction to us. Keep taking the Eliquis exactly as the ER wrote it, two tablets twice a day for the first week then one twice a day. Keeping the 20th is fine. For Thursday: stop every hour or so and walk around for a few minutes. If you get chest pain, trouble breathing, or any bleeding that doesn't stop, go straight to the ER. I've asked the hospital to send me their record.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
New patient, 54 yo woman, transferring care; prior records reviewed (scanned 6/4) and ED record from 6/9 reviewed.

HPI: Seen in the ED 11 days ago for L calf pain/swelling after a long drive; duplex showed L popliteal DVT and she was started on apixaban. Finished the 10 mg loading week on 6/16 and is now on 5 mg twice a day, no missed doses. Swelling is down a lot, calf still a little sore at the end of a long day. No bruising problems, no blood in urine or stool, no chest symptoms or breathlessness. Made the client drive last week with stops.

Diabetes about 9 years, metformin 1000 BID, tolerates it. Checks sugars a few mornings a week, mostly 120s-140s per her. HTN on lisinopril 10, home cuff readings fine. RA for many years on prednisone 5 mg every morning; hands are quiet on that and she's been on the same dose a long time. Her former office wrote the prednisone.

PMH/PSH/FH/SH as in the records summary: TAH 2010, R CTR 2015. Father had a leg clot at 62, mother RA, maternal grandmother T2DM. Never smoker, a glass or two of wine weekly, travels a lot for work as a regional sales manager. Divorced, lives alone.

Meds: apixaban 5 mg BID, metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 10 mg daily, prednisone 5 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: Well appearing. Vitals reviewed. HEENT normal. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear bilaterally. Abd soft, nontender. L calf mildly fuller than R, nontender now, no erythema; trace ankle edema L. R leg normal. Hands: no synovitis today, no deformity. Feet: skin intact, monofilament and vibration normal, DP/PT pulses 2+ both sides. Skin no rash.

PHQ-9: 2.

Assessment/plan:
1. L popliteal DVT, provoked by prolonged travel, 6/9/25. Apixaban 5 mg BID, plan 3 months total, revisit in September. Discussed travel precautions.
2. T2DM: A1c, CMP, lipids, urine microalbumin today. Continue metformin. Eye exam referral to optometry.
3. HTN: at goal on lisinopril, continue.
4. RA on chronic prednisone 5 mg: continue; I'll take over the prescription.
5. Health maintenance: colonoscopy 2021 normal, next 2031. Status post hysterectomy, no Pap needed. Mammogram ordered. Hep C and HIV screen today. Flu/COVID/pneumonia and shingles vaccines in the fall.

Follow up in about 3 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Valerie, your labs from Friday are back. A1c is a little above where I'd like it but reasonable; let's see where it is in September. Kidney and liver tests are normal, blood counts normal, urine protein normal. Cholesterol panel is fine. Hepatitis C and HIV screens are negative. No changes for now.

reports.text: Bilateral screening mammogram with tomosynthesis. Comparison: none available. The breasts are heterogeneously dense, which may obscure small masses. No suspicious mass, architectural distortion or suspicious calcifications in either breast. Skin and nipples are unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: BI-RADS 1, negative. Routine screening in 1 year.

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Here to close out the clot. Three months of apixaban done as of this week, took it faithfully. Leg back to normal, no swelling even after long drives, no pain. No bleeding issues. Sugars at home similar to before. No new joint flares. Still on the road 3 days a week.

Meds: apixaban 5 BID, metformin 1000 BID, lisinopril 10, prednisone 5.

O: Vitals reviewed, BP at goal. Calves symmetric and soft, no edema, no tenderness either leg. Heart and lungs normal.

A/P:
1. L popliteal DVT, travel-provoked, treated 3 months. Resolved clinically. Stop apixaban today. Reviewed what a recurrence feels like and to call right away if it happens. For long car rides or flights: move every 1-2 hours, stay hydrated, calf exercises.
2. T2DM: A1c and BMP today, continue metformin.
3. HTN controlled.
4. RA on prednisone 5, stable.
Vaccines next month when the fall shots are in. RTC 3 months.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: A1c basically unchanged from June; kidney function and potassium normal. Keep doing what you're doing. Fall vaccine visit with the nurse is set for 10/7.

documents.title: Leg is swollen again
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Sorry to bother you on a holiday weekend. I got back from London on Tuesday and since Wednesday my left leg has been getting bigger and sore again, this time it's going up into the thigh. It feels like last time but worse. What should I do?

documents.title: RE: Leg is swollen again
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Not a bother at all. With your history this needs an ultrasound today and likely a blood thinner right away, and the ER is the fastest way to get both on a holiday Friday. Please go this morning, don't drive yourself if the leg is very painful. If you have any chest pain or shortness of breath call 911. I'll let them know you're coming.

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets (10 mg) by mouth twice daily through 12/7, then 1 tablet (5 mg) twice daily

reports.text: Left lower extremity venous duplex with evaluation of the external iliac vein. Indication: left calf and thigh swelling and pain, prior left popliteal DVT. Comparison: duplex 06/09/2025. The left common femoral vein is expanded, filled with echogenic thrombus and noncompressible; thrombus continues through the femoral vein and the popliteal vein. Thrombus extends cephalad into the left external iliac vein, which shows no detectable flow. Calf veins compress where visualized. The great saphenous vein is patent. Right common femoral vein compressible with normal phasic flow.
reports.conclusion: Acute occlusive deep vein thrombosis of the left external iliac, common femoral, femoral and popliteal veins (iliofemoral DVT).

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary (received)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Department of Internal Medicine. Admitted 11/28/2025, discharged 12/01/2025. Received electronically 12/02/2025.

Admitting diagnosis: left lower extremity swelling.
Discharge diagnosis: acute left iliofemoral deep vein thrombosis, recurrent.

History: 54-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis on prednisone 5 mg daily, and a left popliteal DVT in June 2025 treated with 3 months of apixaban (completed September). Two days of progressive pain and swelling of the left calf and thigh beginning one day after a transatlantic flight; she landed three days before presentation. No trauma. Directed to the ED by her primary care physician.

Exam on admission: vital signs stable. Left calf erythematous, warm, tender to palpation, with pitting edema from the calf down to the ankle; left calf circumference 3 cm larger than right. Pain in the calf with passive dorsiflexion of the foot. Remainder unremarkable.

Data: CBC within normal limits. Creatinine 1.0 mg/dL. D-dimer 2.6 mg/L FEU (ref <0.5). Venous duplex: occlusive thrombus from the left external iliac vein through the common femoral, femoral and popliteal veins.

Hospital course: Started on weight-based enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously every 12 hours. Leg elevated, pain controlled with acetaminophen. Swelling and pain improved over 72 hours, ambulating without difficulty. No signs of pulmonary embolism. Transitioned to apixaban at discharge. Given a second venous thrombosis, the team recommends indefinite anticoagulation with periodic review of bleeding risk.

Discharge medications: apixaban 10 mg twice daily through 12/07, then 5 mg twice daily (NEW); metformin 1000 mg twice daily; lisinopril 10 mg daily; prednisone 5 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Problem list per hospital: acute DVT of left popliteal vein; iliofemoral DVT; type 2 diabetes; hypertension; rheumatoid arthritis.

Follow-up: primary care within 1 week.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Post-hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Seen 4 days after discharge for a L iliofemoral DVT (admitted 11/28-12/1; discharge summary reviewed). Second clot in 6 months, this one after a long flight home from overseas.

She feels much better. Thigh swelling mostly gone, calf still heavier by evening. Walking normally. On apixaban 10 mg BID until Sunday, then 5 mg BID; knows the switch date. No bleeding. No chest pain or breathlessness.

Exam: Vitals reviewed. L thigh soft, L calf mildly swollen, minimal tenderness, no erythema. Lungs clear. Heart regular.

A/P:
1. Recurrent L leg DVT, now iliofemoral. Agree with hospital: anticoagulation indefinitely. Will review yearly for bleeding risk. Gave her a written plan for flights: aisle seat, get up hourly, fluids. Bleeding precautions reviewed; avoid NSAIDs, Tylenol is fine for the leg. CBC and BMP today to check counts and kidney function on apixaban.
2. T2DM, HTN, RA: no changes. A1c due next visit.
Will need a new PA on apixaban for 2026 - MA to start it. RTC early March, sooner for any new swelling.

documents.title: Chronic Care Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Follow-up for diabetes, BP and the clot. Rescheduled from last week.

Doing well. Leg back to baseline, only a bit of heaviness on travel days; getting up on flights as planned. On apixaban 5 BID, maybe missed 2 doses this winter, no bleeding beyond a nick shaving. No chest pain or breathlessness. Diet slipped over the holidays she says, back on track now. Morning sugars 120s-150s. RA quiet on prednisone 5.

Meds: apixaban 5 mg BID; metformin 1000 mg BID; lisinopril 10 mg daily; prednisone 5 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: Vitals reviewed, BP at goal. L calf slightly larger than R, soft, nontender, no edema. Heart RRR, lungs clear. Feet: skin intact, sensation normal, pulses good.

A/P:
1. T2DM: A1c, BMP today. Continue metformin, revisit if A1c creeping.
2. HTN: controlled on lisinopril.
3. Recurrent L leg DVT on indefinite apixaban: CBC today. Tolerating well.
4. RA on prednisone 5 mg daily.
5. Shingrix #2 today (RN). Mammogram due July.
RTC June for the yearly labs.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Valerie, labs look stable: blood counts and kidney function normal on the apixaban, potassium fine. A1c is up a little from the fall, which fits the holidays you mentioned; let's recheck in June before changing anything.

Routine 3-month visit plus yearly labs.

Feeling fine today. Busy quarter at work, a lot of driving, taking breaks as we discussed. No leg swelling beyond her usual mild heaviness on the left. No bleeding. Taking all meds; prednisone 5 every morning for years now, RA under control. No hypoglycemia. PHQ-2 0.

Meds: apixaban 5 mg BID; metformin 1000 mg BID; lisinopril 10 mg daily; prednisone 5 mg daily. NKDA.

Exam: Vitals reviewed, at goal. Comfortable. Heart RRR, lungs clear, abdomen soft and nontender. L calf a touch fuller than R, nontender. Feet: monofilament intact, pulses 2+, skin fine.

A/P:
1. T2DM: A1c, CMP, lipids, urine microalbumin today. Optometry eye exam due August, she'll schedule.
2. HTN: controlled, continue lisinopril.
3. Recurrent L leg DVT: on long-term apixaban, doing well; CBC today.
4. RA on chronic prednisone 5 mg: continue.
5. Mammogram due next month, order to be placed with results.
RTC 3 months, early September.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary (received)
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
Regional hospital, Internal Medicine (ICU then medical floor). Admitted 06/12/2026, discharged 06/17/2026. Received electronically 06/18/2026; filed for PCP review.

Principal diagnosis: adrenal crisis.
Other: type 2 diabetes; hypertension; rheumatoid arthritis on long-term glucocorticoid; recurrent left lower extremity DVT on apixaban.

Presentation: 55-year-old woman who slipped and fell at home in the afternoon. Within a couple of hours she developed abrupt, severe abdominal pain with repeated vomiting. Did not hit her head, no loss of consciousness. In the ED: BP 85/50, HR 110, afebrile. Abdomen tender to palpation without rebound or guarding. Na 130, K 5.5, BUN 25, creatinine 1.2, glucose 92, WBC 12.0. Pressure remained low despite an initial normal saline bolus.

Course: Given chronic prednisone use and refractory hypotension, adrenal crisis was diagnosed and hydrocortisone 100 mg IV was given in the ED, followed by 50 mg IV every 6 hours. Systolic pressure rose above 100 within a few hours. Admitted to the ICU for monitoring. CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast, done given abdominal pain on anticoagulation, showed no acute findings and no bleeding; normal adrenal glands. Apixaban was held until the CT was read, then resumed. Lisinopril and metformin were held on admission. Vomiting stopped overnight, eating by day 2, transferred to the floor on day 2. Hydrocortisone tapered and converted to oral prednisone 10 mg daily. Electrolytes and renal function normalized: on 06/17 Na 136, K 4.3, creatinine 0.9. Lisinopril and metformin restarted before discharge with pressures and sugars stable.

Discharge medications: prednisone 10 mg daily for 5 days, then back to 5 mg daily (CHANGED, temporary); hydrocortisone sodium succinate 100 mg IM emergency injection kit (NEW); apixaban 5 mg twice daily; metformin 1000 mg twice daily; lisinopril 10 mg daily.
Allergies: NKDA.

Education: steroid sick-day rules (double the prednisone dose for fever or acute illness, use the emergency injection and call 911 if vomiting and unable to keep the dose down); never stop prednisone abruptly.

Follow-up: endocrinology referral placed by the inpatient team; primary care after discharge.

documents.title: Home from the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Just wanted you to know I was in the hospital since last Friday, a few hours after I saw you. I fell in the kitchen and then got really sick, they said it was an adrenal crisis from the prednisone. I'm home since yesterday and feeling a lot better, just tired. They gave me an emergency shot to keep at home. Do I need to come in? I have a work trip I can't move the first week of July and then I'm on vacation until late August.

documents.title: RE: Home from the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Valerie, I'm so sorry, and glad you're home. I have the hospital summary. Take the prednisone exactly as they wrote it, 10 mg for the five days and then back to your usual 5 mg, and keep the injection kit with you when you travel. If you get a fever, a stomach bug, or start vomiting, follow the sick-day rules they gave you and call us. Our nurse will call you Monday to go over everything. Please keep the endocrinology appointment they set up. I'd still like to see you in person after your trips; the front desk will reach out to book.

documents.title: Post-discharge call
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt after 6/12-6/17 admission for adrenal crisis. Reports feeling close to normal, energy coming back, no vomiting, eating well, no dizziness on standing. Finished the 5 days of prednisone 10 mg this weekend, back to 5 mg this morning. Has the hydrocortisone IM kit and watched the hospital's teaching video; knows when to use it. Sick-day rules reviewed again, she repeated them back. Taking apixaban, metformin, lisinopril as before. Endocrinology appt 7/24 confirmed. She declined an in-person visit before her July travel. Front desk to book PCP follow-up for after Labor Day per her schedule.

documents.title: Follow-up booked
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Booked hospital follow-up/diabetes visit 9/4 at 10:00, first date she's back and available. Pt aware she can text or call sooner if anything changes.

documents.title: Endocrinology Consultation (received)
documents.author: endocrinology
documents.body:
Outside endocrinology group. Date of service 07/24/2026. Received by fax 07/28/2026.

Reason for referral: adrenal crisis 06/2026.

Thank you for the referral of Ms. Labrie, 55, who has taken prednisone 5 mg daily for many years for rheumatoid arthritis. In June she had a fall at home followed by abdominal pain, vomiting and hypotension with hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, which responded promptly to IV hydrocortisone; CT showed normal adrenals and no hemorrhage. She completed a brief 10 mg prednisone course and has been on 5 mg daily since. She feels well, back at work, no lightheadedness, salt craving, nausea or weight change.

Medications: prednisone 5 mg daily; apixaban 5 mg twice daily; metformin 1000 mg twice daily; lisinopril 10 mg daily; hydrocortisone 100 mg IM emergency kit.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.

Exam: vitals reviewed, not orthostatic. Well appearing. Remainder unremarkable.

Impression: adrenal insufficiency due to long-term glucocorticoid therapy, with adrenal crisis precipitated by acute illness. She should be regarded as steroid dependent.

Recommendations:
1. Continue prednisone 5 mg each morning; do not stop or taper without guidance.
2. Sick-day rules reviewed: double the dose for fever or acute illness for the duration of illness; emergency IM hydrocortisone 100 mg and emergency care if vomiting or unable to take oral doses.
3. Stress-dose steroid coverage for surgery or procedures; please share this letter with any surgical team.
4. Medical alert bracelet or ID advised.
5. Follow up here in 6 months.
